stories.headline: Vance-led task force set to unveil charges against 40-plus defendants in alleged $40M SNAP fraud
stories.note: The administration's fraud crackdown is delivering real charges on a big-dollar welfare scheme.
body: Vice President JD Vance is set to announce Wednesday that the federal anti-fraud task force he runs has tied more than 40 suspects to about $40 million in alleged food-stamp fraud, with criminal charges to be unveiled, Fox News Digital reported first.

The new cases push the task force's total uncovered SNAP fraud to $641 million. More than 1,000 retailers have been kicked out of the program for offenses like trafficking benefits, and close to 5,000 more were suspended and fined a combined $44 million.

Officials also say they've destroyed over 2,200 illegal card-reader devices and shut off more than 2,000 compromised retailer numbers, moves they estimate blocked more than $5 billion in possible fraudulent transactions. Across all programs, the task force reports $260.7 billion in fraud uncovered since Trump took office.

Charges don't guarantee the money comes back. Vance has acknowledged that recovery is tough, saying "once it's gone out the door, it's very hard to get it back," which is why the focus is on stopping payments up front.
The announcement follows Tuesday's Oval Office rollout of a whistleblower program that pays tipsters a 1% commission on fraud they help expose.
Why it matters: Republicans get a concrete, dollar-figure story on protecting taxpayers, while Democrats are pushed onto the defensive over how welfare programs were policed.

stories.headline: Trump says Ilhan Omar could go to jail or be deported, calls her 'a disgrace to our country'
stories.note: Trump keeps the spotlight on the mounting federal scrutiny around one of the Democrats' best-known progressives.
body: President Trump said Tuesday that Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., could face jail, not just deportation, as federal investigators look into allegations about her citizenship. He called her "a disgrace to our country" during an Oval Office event on his new fraud-tip program.
Asked by FOX Business about possible deportation, Trump said, "She could also go to jail," while noting it was his opinion. He didn't name a specific charge or offer new evidence.

The probe centers on whether Omar's birth year was misstated on immigration paperwork, which affects whether she qualified for citizenship through her father in 2000. Federal agents searched her Washington home Oct. 12 and took her phone.
Border czar Tom Homan has said someone who lies during naturalization can be denaturalized, and that he's been told investigators have a strong case.

Omar denies wrongdoing, and she and Democrats including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries call the investigation political persecution before the midterms. Trump closed by saying he hoped she'd be treated fairly.
Why it matters: The Omar investigation keeps one of the left's most polarizing figures at the center of the news, which Republicans see as a gift heading into November.

stories.headline: Winery owned by Ilhan Omar's husband shuttered due to fraud, James Comer says
stories.note: House Oversight Chair Comer adds a new fraud angle to the Omar saga.
body: House Oversight Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., says a California winery co-owned by Rep. Ilhan Omar's husband, Tim Mynett, was shut down amid fraud claims, including allegations it sold investors empty barrels billed as wine to be aged.
Speaking on Fox News' "Sunday Night in America," Comer said his committee's look at Omar's financial disclosures turned up multiple grounds where a search warrant could be justified.

The winery, eStCru, closed in April. Omar's 2023 disclosure valued her stake at $15,001 to $50,000, but the next year's form put it at $1,000,001 to $5,000,000, a jump Comer questioned in a February letter. Omar told the Wall Street Journal in April that she and her husband have under $100,000 combined.

Lawyers for Mynett and his business partner said any suggestion they deliberately defrauded investors would be false and defamatory. Oversight referred the matter to the House Ethics Committee, which hasn't taken it up yet.
Why it matters: On top of the citizenship probe, the money questions give Republicans another line of attack on Omar and on Democrats who've rallied to defend her.

stories.headline: On the streets with Dr Oz as surprise fraud crackdown sends daycare directors scrambling
stories.note: Dr. Oz's surprise visits show the GOP taking taxpayer-fraud enforcement door to door.
body: CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz personally confronted staff at two senior day-care centers in Flushing, Queens, on Tuesday over suspected Medicaid overbilling, with Fox News Digital along for an exclusive look.

The visits to Kent Senior Care and Evergreen Adult Day Care were part of a wider New York City sweep in which CMS officials made more than 80 visits and delivered warning letters, working alongside the FBI, the HHS inspector general's office and the NYPD.

At Kent, Oz told the director the bills looked like the center was "completely full all the time" even though it didn't appear crowded, and questioned charges for five-day attendance and wheelchair transport. The director insisted the center bills only for seniors who actually attend and uses sign-in sheets.

Oz said the broader crackdown includes arrests, search warrants and moves to cut off certain operators from Medicaid billing, though Fox didn't witness those actions. Kent declined comment and Evergreen didn't respond.
Why it matters: Seeing a top Trump health official go door to door after suspected fraud in a deep-blue city reinforces the GOP message that it's serious about protecting taxpayer money.

stories.headline: Virginia sanctuary county ignores 1,670 detainer requests over 2 years, House Judiciary Committee finds
stories.note: House Republicans put hard numbers on the cost of Democrat-run sanctuary policies.
body: A new House Judiciary Committee report says the Fairfax County, Virginia, sheriff's office ignored at least 1,670 ICE detainer requests from 2023 to 2025, releasing criminal illegal immigrants instead of handing them over to federal custody.

The report, led by Chairman Jim Jordan and subcommittee chair Tom McClintock, also accuses Commonwealth's Attorney Steve Descano of treating illegal-immigrant defendants more leniently than citizens to shield them from immigration consequences. A review of more than 1,100 cases flagged over 100 previously unreported illegal immigrants who benefited.

It says Descano's office rarely pursued charges like DUI, felony drug possession, grand larceny and assaulting an officer, and that many defendants went on to reoffend, some violently. It also alleges he misled Congress about his policies.

The report highlights the February stabbing death of Stephanie Minter; the suspect, an illegal immigrant, had more than 40 prior charges in the county. Her mother told the committee that "a system failed my daughter." Descano rejects the allegations.
Why it matters: Republicans now have hard numbers and a heartbreaking case to make sanctuary policies a defining issue against Democrats this fall.

stories.headline: Bruce Blakeman hammers Dem Gov Hochul, Mamdani over subway safety during NYC campaign ride
stories.note: The GOP's New York governor candidate takes the crime fight straight to Hochul and Mamdani on the subway.
body: Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman rode the New York City subway Monday and called Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul the "most pro-criminal governor" in the country, pinning rising subway crime on her and Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Blakeman, the Nassau County executive and a former Port Authority commissioner, said riders keep telling him they feel less safe. His plan includes more police, more conductors, better lighting and getting emotionally ill people the help they need instead of leaving them in the system.

He also hit congestion pricing as a tax on the middle class and criticized Hochul for her December 2025 veto of a bill requiring two-person crews on more trains. Hochul argued that bill would slow MTA modernization and cost up to $10 million a year.
The ride came days after a man was shot and killed on the subway, with NYPD releasing a photo of the suspect.
Why it matters: Taking the crime message straight into deep-blue New York City shows Blakeman wants to make public safety the deciding issue against Hochul.
